Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old man with known asthma presenting with 3 hours of acute chest tightness, wheeze, nonproductive cough and mild exertional shortness of breath after a recent upper respiratory infection; clinician treated as an asthma exacerbation and arranged inhalers, oral steroid course and spacer with safety-netting.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Acute chest tightness for ~3 hours described as inability to get a full breath.
  - Associated cough (non-productive) and wheeze.
  - Mild shortness of breath, worse with exertion (stairs), not short of breath at rest.
- Timeline:
  - Recent viral upper respiratory infection last week (sore throat, runny nose) that is improving; cough and wheeze have persisted.
  - Patient ran out of his inhalers approximately 1 week ago while away at university and has not had them since.
  - Current chest tightness started ~3 hours prior to consult.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Exacerbated by exertion and at night (worse at night).
  - No specific relieving factors documented; has not used bronchodilator this week because ran out.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - Wheeze, cough, mild exertional dyspnea.
  - No spitting up of sputum reported.
  - No chest pain (patient describes tightness but not pain), no hemoptysis, no documented fever.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - Not short of breath at rest.
  - No recent hospitalization except remote history in adolescence.
  - No drug allergies.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma
  - Longstanding; severe exacerbation in adolescence (~age 16–17) requiring hospital admission and endotracheal intubation.
- Atopy/allergies:
  - Hayfever; allergic to dust.
  - Childhood eczema and milk protein allergy.
- No other chronic conditions reported.

Medications:
- Inhaled salbutamol (Ventolin) — patient uses it; currently has run out and not with him for ~1 week. (dose/route/frequency not documented)
  - Clinician advised salbutamol as PRN inhaler.
- Inhaled corticosteroid Clenil Modulite — patient uses it; currently ran out and not with him for ~1 week. (dose/route/frequency not documented)
  - Clinician advised Clenil use in the morning as maintenance.
- Oral corticosteroid tablets prescribed during consult: two tablets each morning for 5 days — agent/name not documented.
- Spacer to be provided.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies. Environmental/allergic history as above.

Social History:
- Student (was away at university when inhalers ran out).
- Smoking, alcohol, and illicit drug use not documented.
- No other social/financial concerns documented aside from being away from home/university travel leading to running out of meds.

Family History:
- Father: asthma.
- Mother: eczema.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded.

Investigations:
- No investigations, imaging or peak flow performed or ordered during this consult.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation (most likely triggered by recent viral upper respiratory infection and medication omission). This aligns with the provided DDx which ranks asthma exacerbation as most likely.

DDx Integration (brief):
- 1) Acute asthma exacerbation — High likelihood.
  - Supporting: Known asthma with prior severe attack, current wheeze, chest tightness, nonproductive cough, recent URTI, and ran out of inhaled steroid and SABA ~1 week ago.
  - Opposing: Patient is not short of breath at rest and can ambulate; no objective measurements (PEF, O2).
- 2) Viral bronchitis / post-viral reactive airways — Medium likelihood.
  - Supporting: Recent cold last week with persistent cough and wheeze.
  - Opposing: Preexisting asthma and missed inhalers favor primary asthma exacerbation.
- 3) Community-acquired pneumonia — Low–medium likelihood.
  - Supporting: Possible post-viral bacterial infection.
  - Opposing: No fever, no productive cough, no focal chest pain or focal exam findings recorded.

Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation (primary)
- Assessment:
  - Probable asthma exacerbation precipitated by recent viral URTI and discontinuation/omission of inhaled therapy for ~1 week. Currently not in apparent life-threatening distress per history.
- Plan:
  - Prescribe inhalers: salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler for PRN use and Clenil Modulite inhaler for daily morning use — dose/route/frequency for each not documented in transcript (prescription to be sent by clinician).
  - Provide spacer and instruction on use; clinician to send spacer.
  - Oral corticosteroid course prescribed: two tablets each morning for 5 days — specific agent/name not documented (patient instructed to read medication label for side effects).
  - Safety-netting:
    - Advise to seek urgent medical attention if worsening shortness of breath, increased work of breathing, chest pain, light-headedness, or if using salbutamol more frequently than every 3 hours.
    - If symptoms do not improve or worsen, present to emergency services or primary care for reassessment (peak flow, oxygen, exam).
  - Return/follow-up:
    - Arrange follow-up if symptoms persist or worsen; clinician anticipated sending prescriptions within ~1 hour.
    - Time off work/school recommended until improved; clinician noted patient can self-certify for first 7 days.

Issue 2: Viral bronchitis / post-viral wheeze
- Assessment:
  - Possible concurrent post-viral airway hyperreactivity contributing to symptoms.
- Plan:
  - Conservative/supportive management as above (bronchodilator, inhaled steroid, oral steroid short course).
  - No antibiotics indicated in absence of fever, purulent sputum or systemic toxicity.
  - Reassess if fever, productive sputum, or clinical deterioration develops.

Issue 3: Community-acquired pneumonia / other alternative causes (lower likelihood)
- Assessment:
  - Consider if clinical picture evolves (fever, focal chest signs, productive cough or persistent deterioration).
- Plan:
  - If concerning features develop, obtain chest x-ray and consider further investigations (O2 sats, blood tests) and possible antibiotics based on clinical assessment.
  - Consider alternative diagnoses (PE, anxiety) if atypical features or lack of improvement — not felt likely currently.

General plan items:
- Education on inhaler and spacer technique; encourage use of spacer to improve drug delivery.
- Counsel on short-term steroid side effects and to read medication label; reassurance provided regarding usual tolerance.
- Prescriptions to be sent to patient; spacer to be sent.
- Clear safety-netting instructions provided (see Issue 1).

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: No vitals recorded; no physical examination findings documented; no peak expiratory flow or pulse oximetry measured; smoking status and baseline inhaler doses not documented; specific names/doses/routes for inhaler prescriptions and exact oral steroid agent not documented.
- Conflicts: No direct conflicts noted between transcript and DDx; DDx supports the transcript impression (conflict noted: none).
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor audio cut-out during part of steroid side-effect discussion but clinical content intelligible.
